newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-PIERCE THE LAST LOCAL DISH ON FRENCH MENU.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-PIERCE THE LAST LOCAL DISH ON FRENCH MENU.

text.p: With the exception of Mary Pierce, the Gallic flavour has been squeezed out of the French Open as the Grand Slam event heads towards its second week.

The host nation's hopes of seeing one of their own lift a title were reduced to the women's 10th seed, as the remaining members of the 34-strong French contingent were blown away on a breezy Parisian afternoon.
France has not cheered a local champion since 1983 when Yannick Noah claimed the men's crown.

The day began badly with Nathalie Tauziat crashing out in straight sets to three-times champion Monica Seles, and ended the same way with Davis Cup hero Arnaud Boetsch falling to Chile's Marcelo Rios.

In between, Stephane Simian became the third French scalp claimed by American Michael Chang when he limped off court with a groin injury while Pierce advanced at the expense of compatriot Sandrine Testud.
With Pierce due to face Seles in Sunday's last centre court match, Gallic involvement could easily end before the start of the second week.
The match shapes up as an intriguing contest between two of the hardest hitters in the women's game.
Pierce won their last encounter, edging past the American 7-6 7-6 in Rome earlier this year.
"That was my first time playing her since she was stabbed and anyone could have won that match," said Pierce, a French finalist in 1994.
"I'm looking forward to playing her again. I love the challenge.
"She stays in the rally a little bit longer and maybe isn't as quick, but she's still a tough opponent and one of the best players out there."
Said Seles: "It was a very weird match in Rome. Hopefully I can improve on that, not just the outcome but the way I played.
"Mary is different than anyone I've played here this week.
"She hits the ball very hard, so it will be fast tennis. I can't play defensively, she'll just blow me off the court."
Pierce, who has enjoyed a turbulent relationship with the Parisian crowd, has not always been able to count on their support.
Born in Canada and raised in the United States, she has never been totally accepted by her adopted country, the French more than once booing her off the court -- even after she has won.

The 1995 Australian Open champion says she doesn't hear the whistles, but like everyone else Parisians love a winner and if she can become the first French champion since Francoise Durr in 1967 all will be forgiven.
